subject: physics
question_text: State Newton’s third law of motion. Give one example.

verification.note: PREDICTED — Session 89 enumeration sweep (archetype × object grid over the NCERT chapter): this question has not appeared in any paper or source book we hold, but the chapter contains it and the 2-mark/4-mark format admits it. Authored as a lean card; promote to a full card when a paper season or a Telangana IPE teacher validates the cell. Split invented, as everywhere.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The statement
lines: To every action there is an equal and
The two forces are equal in magnitude,
opposite in direction, and act on TWO
steps.why: The "two different bodies" clause is the whole law; without it the pair would cancel and nothing could ever move.
common_mistakes: Saying the action and reaction cancel each other — they act on different bodies, so they never do.

recall.must_convey: That action and reaction are equal and opposite and act on two different bodies.

steps.memory_tip: Write it as F(A on B) and F(B on A). The two bodies are then visible in the notation.
steps.margin_note: First mark. All three parts — equal, opposite, and acting on two different bodies.

steps.label: The example
lines: The foot pushes the ground backwards
steps.why: The reaction is the force that actually does the useful work, which is why the pair being on different bodies matters.
common_mistakes: Naming a single force as the example instead of naming both of the pair.

recall.must_convey: That the foot pushes the ground backwards and the ground pushes the foot forwards.

steps.memory_tip: On smooth ice the ground cannot push the foot forward. Walking fails without that reaction.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name both forces of the pair. A single force is not an example of this law.

insider_note: The example carries a full mark, equal to the statement. Name both forces of the pair and the two bodies they act on.
